# Brick-based storage and caching
Also called: bricking, brick caching, brick-based raycasting

## Overview
Brick-based storage and caching decomposes a dense volume dataset into fixed-size, power-of-two cubic blocks (bricks) to maximize CPU cache coherency during ray traversal and manage memory for datasets larger than physical RAM [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from linear memory layouts by maintaining nearly constant rendering performance regardless of viewing direction, whereas linear layouts suffer from view-dependent performance degradation [S1, unofficial]. It differs from hierarchical methods like [N³-tree with Brick Pool and Node Pool](3407-n-tree-with-brick-pool-and-node-pool.md) by using a flat or shallow hierarchy with explicit caching policies (e.g., LRU) rather than dynamic LOD traversal via an octree.

## Shared principles
All brick-based implementations share the following mechanisms:

1.  **Domain Discretization into Bricks:** The continuous domain is partitioned into a grid of fixed-size cubic blocks. If the volume dimensions are $D_x, D_y, D_z$ and brick dimensions are $B_x, B_y, B_z$, the number of bricks in each dimension is:
    $$ N_x = \lceil D_x / B_x \rceil, \quad N_y = \lceil D_y / B_y \rceil, \quad N_z = \lceil D_z / B_z \rceil $$
    The total number of bricks is $N_{total} = N_x \cdot N_y \cdot N_z$ [S2, unofficial].
2.  **Linear Memory Mapping:** Bricks are stored in a linear array (or texture) in xyz-order. The index of a brick $(i, j, k)$ is:
    $$ Index(i, j, k) = i + j \cdot N_x + k \cdot N_x \cdot N_y $$
    where $0 \le i < N_x$, $0 \le j < N_y$, $0 \le k < N_z$ [S1, unofficial].
3.  **Boundary Padding:** To support trilinear interpolation at brick boundaries without accessing adjacent bricks, each logical brick of size $(B_x, B_y, B_z)$ is stored with a 1-voxel padding layer on all sides. The stored voxel count per brick is:
    $$ V_{brick} = (B_x+1)(B_y+1)(B_z+1) $$
    [S1, unofficial].
4.  **Cache Residency:** Bricks are not always resident in fast memory (GPU VRAM or CPU cache). A caching mechanism (LRU, multi-level, or hierarchical) manages the mapping from logical brick coordinates to physical memory slots, evicting bricks when capacity is exceeded [S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md)
Manages a fixed-size pool of volume data blocks, mapping logical brick coordinates to physical pool indices and evicting the least-recently-used blocks when the pool is full. It solves the problem of limited GPU memory capacity by ensuring that expensive data transfers from slower host memory are minimized. It sets itself apart by explicitly maintaining a sorted list of blocks along the ray depth for immediate lookup and by decoupling volume size from GPU resolution limits using a low-resolution reference texture. Unlike [N³-tree with Brick Pool and Node Pool](3407-n-tree-with-brick-pool-and-node-pool.md) which uses hierarchical octrees, this method relies on a flat pool with LRU eviction.

### [Brick-based Volume Raycasting](3341-brick-based-volume-raycasting.md)
Defines the specific ray-marching algorithm and addressing scheme required to traverse a one-level subdivision hierarchy of bricks. It solves the view-dependent performance degradation inherent in linear memory layouts while maintaining low memory overhead compared to spread memory layouts. It builds on [Brick-based storage and caching](4138-brick-based-storage-and-caching.md) by defining the traversal logic, including empty brick detection via histograms and padded brick sampling.

### [N³-tree with Brick Pool and Node Pool](3407-n-tree-with-brick-pool-and-node-pool.md)
A hierarchical data structure combining an N³-tree for spatial subdivision with a brick pool for volume data and a node pool for tree structure, allowing efficient level-of-detail (LOD) and visibility culling. It sets itself apart by storing all tree nodes in a single 3D texture (the node pool) with a single pointer per node, reducing memory requirements by 16x compared to Gobbetti et al. [GMAG08] and improving cache coherence. Unlike [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md) which relies on static replacement policies, this method dynamically determines LOD in the shader during traversal.

### [Multi-Level Cache and Prefetching](4631-multi-level-cache-and-prefetching.md)
A memory management strategy utilizing a four-tier caching hierarchy (L2 Disk, L1 Compressed, L0 Decompressed, S-cache Slice) combined with proactive data fetching to hide network latency. It solves the problem of slow interactive performance when accessing large, remote datasets by ensuring frequently accessed data is available in fast memory before it is needed. It differs from [Brick Caching with LRU Replacement](879-brick-caching-with-lru-replacement.md) by explicitly separating compressed and decompressed storage and integrating an S-cache for slice-level acceleration, with prefetching driven by access patterns and idle time.

### [Bricked Volume Hierarchy](5036-bricked-volume-hierarchy.md)
A data organization scheme where a volume dataset is partitioned into chunks called bricks across multiple resolution levels. It solves the problem of managing multi-resolution data for efficient GPU access by decoupling the logical resolution levels from the geometric subdivision of the spatial hierarchy. It sets itself apart by strictly separating the "bricked volume hierarchy" (data chunks and resolution) from the "residency octree" (spatial subdivision and cache residency).

### [Raymarching with LOD-based Brick Caching](5776-raymarching-with-lod-based-brick-caching.md)
Renders Compressed Segmentation Volumes (CSVs) by raymarching with one ray per pixel, dynamically decompressing bricks at the required Level of Detail (LOD) on the GPU. It distinguishes itself by integrating empty-space skipping via palettes before cache allocation, using contiguous base elements instead of superblocks, and allowing a one-frame lag for decompression requests to exploit temporal coherency. It solves the problem of rendering massive segmentation datasets (e.g., >6 GB) interactively by streaming only necessary fine-detail data.

### Cyclic Buffer for Smoke Volume
#### definition
- A cyclic buffer structure used to store layers of smoke volume data, where the first layer (Index 0) is duplicated to the end to enable smooth transitions at the seeding step [S1, unofficial].
- A buffer where the first layer is duplicated to the end to depict cyclic property, allowing overwriting of the oldest layer [S1, unofficial].

#### step
- Each layer has an age relative to the time it was seeded. The oldest layer is overwritten next. When a layer at index 4 is overwritten, it becomes the youngest, and the seeding indicator moves one step forward [S1, unofficial].
- To enable smooth transitions at the seeding step, the volumes of cubic cells between two layers are multiplied by a fade-in/out modifier based on the age of the cell [S1, unofficial].
- Overwrite the oldest layer (indicated by an arrow) with new data, moving the seeding indicator one step forward. The overwritten layer becomes the youngest [S1, unofficial].
- Multiply volumes of cubic cells between two layers by a fade-in/out modifier depending on cell age to enable smooth transitions at the seeding step [S1, unofficial].

### Homogeneous Brick Optimization
#### step
- Nodes corresponding to homogeneous bricks (all voxels contain the same value up to a user-defined threshold) store the average value in the brick instead of a pointer to the brick's location in the brick cache [S2, unofficial].

#### pitfall
- For multi-channel data, a node can only be marked homogeneous if its corresponding bricks in all channels are homogeneous [S2, unofficial].

## Background
Brick-based storage originated as a solution to the memory bandwidth and cache coherency limitations of linear volume rendering. Early implementations focused on CPU-side caching to handle datasets larger than main memory, using LRU policies to manage brick residency [S2, unofficial]. The approach was later adapted for GPU rendering, where the fixed-size bricks align well with texture sampling and cache lines, reducing the view-dependent performance penalties of linear layouts [S1, unofficial]. Variants like the N³-tree and multi-level caches have extended the concept to handle hierarchical LOD and remote data access in web-based renderers [S1, unofficial].
